utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Weekends are becoming dangerous. Unfortunately, Judge Thelin is unable to be with us today but is expected to be able to be here tomorrow. We have decided pursuant to the Rule to continue the hearing with just two Judges. And I see there have been heavy casualties on the Defence bar because of the weekend. Now, Mr. Black, what is it you have in mind for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. What we had proposed to do at the beginning before calling in the next witness is to go through some of the 92 bis materials that's pending for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think Mr. Younis has distribute a couple of binders, one of which says "92 bis Witness Statements" on the end of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The small binder. Is that the one you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's the one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What I would propose to do in just a moment is go through those very rapidly and ask for an exhibit number for each tab, basically. But before I do that, I do note that the Prosecution's fourth motion for admission pursuant to Rule 92 bis is pending. This is a motion that the Defence have not opposed because in fact we spent a lot of time agreeing on these witnesses. I don't know if it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We haven't had any formal notice of that yet, so the time's having to run.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I guess what we can do is do the ones of that been provisionally admitted already and we can leave the rest for later date or if Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If there is in fact consent we're happy to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Perhaps -- I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As you reach them that might be able to be indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay, that's -- I'll take them in order, then. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, there has been extensive discussion between the parties related to those witnesses. They're not a matter of dispute and we are content on behalf of the three accused for those statements to be read in by way of 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Khan, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've got the green light now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Great. The bind in front of everyone contains 21 tabs representing 21 witnesses. Seventeen of those had been provisionally admitted at an earlier date including two that the Trial Chamber had admitted then subject to cross-examination. And we have since been able to reach agreement with counsel for the accused for those witness statements to be admitted without cross-examination. And then there are four witnesses who are subject to the motion which I believe is still pending today but to which the Defence have agreed. Before I go through them individually, you will notice that there are redactions in many of them. Those redactions fall into three categories. First, information exclude by the Trial Chamber in its previous decisions; second, some additional redactions agreed with the Defence; and finally, some very small redactions of personal information, specifically identity cards numbers and street addresses were those -- were included in the materials. You will also notice that there are translations into English and Albanian, I believe of all the materials. In some instances those were included in the actual 92 bis packet itself when the attestation was done. At other times, the translation was not included in that but we provide it had and it's behind the tab. So everything should be here in English and Albanian. Now, with Your Honour's permission I'll go quickly through the binder. Well, first, actually, because of the different number of ERN numbers with translations and so forth, it might be a good idea is to admit the index as an exhibit although obviously it's not evidence, but rather than me reading off all of the ERN numbers, I would propose putting the exhibit in as the first exhibit so that the record's clear. I don't know what Your Honour thinks about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just checking that the registry officer has a copy of the list dated 4th of April. The list will be received not as an exhibit but as an index to the individual statements which we are now to deal with, and the reference to the ERN number need not be said as you deal with each statement. You can do it by reference to the number on the list, that is number 1, if you're able that name the witness or the witness's code number as appropriate, but no need to refer to the ERN number. That can be picked up from the index list.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Your Honour. And should the index be given a number so it will be in the record as a reference in the future or how will that work?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will have an MFI number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification as P176.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Then I'll move on. The first -- behind tab 1 are the materials for Witness L-86. I would ask that they be given the next Prosecution number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received and given number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P177, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Behind tab 2 are the materials for Witness L-29. I ask that those receive the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P178.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Behind tab 3 are the materials for Witness L-13.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P179.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Behind tab 4 are the materials for Witness L-34.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P180.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Behind tab 5 are the materials for Witness L-25.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P181.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, if I'm -- no, sorry. It's the next one, L-09.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: L-09. Yes, Your Honour. This is one of the two I mentioned. By the decision of 13 October 2004, the Trial Chamber had provisionally admitted his evidence subject to cross-examination. Now, after that decision, we've had extensive conversations with Defence counsel, and they have agreed to admission of his written evidence without cross-examination. He's one of two witnesses like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I was going to save this for the end but I would like to say it now, we would like to express our gratitude to counsel for the Defence, who have on many of these witnesses gone to great lengths I think to help us, to work with us to reach agreement, which has saved a lot of time in terms of motion practice, and of course of calling witnesses for live testimony. I think while protecting the rights of their clients they've done a lot to reach agreement and move this case along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber is grateful to both Prosecuting and Defence counsel that agreement has been able to be reached in respect of so many matters. It will clearly facilitate the speed with which the trial can be concluded. With respect to this witness, the Chamber would vary its previous order so that it might be admitted without cross-examination in view of the consent of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Bearing in mind that decision now orally given, I would ask that the materials behind tab 6 for Witness L-09 receive the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab number 6 would be P182.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Behind tab 7 are the materials for Witness L-37, whose evidence was provisionally admitted by a decision of 13 October 2004. I ask that it receive the next exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab number 7 would be P183.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next tab, tab 8, the materials for Witness L-15, this is one of the witnesses who is subject to the pending motion which we discussed earlier in the day. We have reached agreement on the admission of this evidence subject to some redactions which have been made and which are included in the version here in the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the redacted form pursuant to Rule 92 bis, the Chamber will receive this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would ask, then, it be given the next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab number 8 would be P184.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Behind tab 9 are the materials for Witness L-8, provisionally admitted on the 17th of February, 2005, and I would ask that they receive the next number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 9 would be P185.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Behind tab 10 are the materials for Witness L-18, also provisionally admitted on the 17th of February, 2005. I would ask they receive the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 10 would be P186.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Tab 11 includes materials for Witness L-28, provisionally admitted on the 13th of October, 2004. I would ask they receive the next number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 11 would be P187.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next tab, tab 12, includes the materials for a Witness L-47. This is another we have reached agreement with the Defence and it's subject to the pending motion, Prosecution's fourth motion for admission pursuant to Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In view of the consent of the Defence, this will be received pursuant to Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Would I ask that have the next number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab number 12 would be P188.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Behind tab 13 are materials for Witness L-48, provisionally admitted on the 13th of October, 2004. I would ask they receive the next number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab number 13 would be P189.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Tab 14 includes materials for Witness L-65, also admitted on the 13th of October, 2004. I would ask they receive the next number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab number 14 would be P190.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The next tab, tab 15, the materials for Witness L-96, this is, Your Honour, another we've agreed with the Defence subject to some redactions which are included here in this binder, and it's subject to the pending motion for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. And this is a witness not on your original witness list; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. Mr. Younis tells me that I may have an incorrect witness number. With the Court's indulgence if I could just check. Mr. Younis corrects me that this witness's number is actually L-98.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that was spotted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Younis to be commended.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: As always. The name, however, on the index is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, in view of the consent of the Defence, that will be received pursuant to Rule 92 bis, and your witness will be amended to add that name.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be -- tab number 15 would be P191.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Next tab, tab 16, includes materials for Witness L-39 provisionally admitted on 13 October 2004. I would ask it receive the next number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab number 16 would be P192.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Tab 17 includes materials for Witness L-93. This is another witness upon whom we've agreed with the Defence and is subject to the pending motion for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: With the consent of the Defence this will be received pursuant to Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab number 17 would be P193.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Tab 18 includes materials for Witness L-83, admitted on the -- provisionally admitted on the 13th of October, 2004. I ask it receive the next number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab number 18 would be Prosecution Exhibit P194.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for the confusion on this, but Mr. Younis is watching me like a hawk, and he tells me that tab 16, although the name is correct the witness number should be L-30. I assure you he is in the process of double-checking my work to make sure that I haven't made any other errors like that. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: L-30 instead of L-39; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For number 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Tab 19, Your Honour, includes materials for Witness L-22, admitted provisionally on the 17th of February, 2005. I ask it receive the next number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 19 would be P195.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Tab 20 includes materials for Witness L-21, provisionally admitted on the 17th of February, 2005. I ask that it receive the next number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab number 20 would be P196.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the final tab, tab 21, includes materials for L-84 [Realtime transcript read in error: "24"]. Your Honour, this is another witness that by decision of 13 October 2004 Your Honours had provisionally admitted it had pursuant to cross-examination. Subsequent to that we reached agreement with the Defence it be admitted without cross-examination. So I move Your Honours to vary the prior order to allow admission without cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Transcript says you mention this as Witness L-24.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: L-84 is what I should have said if I didn't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't know what you said, I merely noticed the transcript and your list.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: L-84. It will be received and the previous order will be varied to allow its admission without cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab number 21 would be P197.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. It's been a bit of housekeeping, but I hope that they have been 20 or 25 minutes well spent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: To be able to receive evidence of 21 witnesses without the need to call them is a significant step for the purposes of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to give you advance warning, there are, I believe, about half a dozen other witnesses, some of which you've already provisionally admitted their evidence, others which we will shortly file a motion for and we hope that we'll be able to reach agreement as we have with these and move their admission within -- well, certainly within the next two weeks. Your Honour, unless you have further questions for me on this topic, I'll turn the floor over to Mr. Shin, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Shin. Thank you very much for that, Mr. Black. Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution is ready for its next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: While we wait for the witness to come in, I may just point out that there are two documents which I provided to the Court assistant to assist -- I can address that later or now if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. If it's of any assistance to the Court, the witness who has presently been called as a witness who the Defence has previously indicated they agree to having his reports submitted and there is not the necessity for any live testimony, however I believe the Prosecution has take a bit of a different tack. So you can assume that unless there is some radical differences between what we believe is going to occur there will be little if no cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And there can be some liberty with leading by the sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Good afternoon, sir. If you would please read allowed the affirmation on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just briefly with the -- there are two pieces of -- two documents, one constituting one page, the second two pages, which we have prepared to assist in following the evidence of this witness. The first document constituting one page is a guide cross-referencing what are called NN numbers which the results of DNA tests and that comes -- that is extracted directly from Prosecution Exhibit P112.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And we of course are not seek to go tender this into evidence but merely to provide it as a guide for following the evidence of the witness. The second document is a two-page document which has columns numbered 1 through 53 providing a brief description with ERN number of certain slides which the witness may be referring to. I don't believe the witness will be referring to all the slides, but all the better perhaps to have a guide so if we move around it will be easier to follow. And copies have been provided to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Maat.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you please tell the Court your full name.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: George.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So that would be George Maat?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And when were you born?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: I'm full professor of anatomy and forensic anthropology at the Leiden University Medical Center.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And I believe you prepared for the Office of the Prosecutor a report dated the 13th of August, 2003; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What is it the Prosecution requested for you to do for that report?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: I was asked to go to Kosovo and look for skeletons which had been excavated two years before to see if injuries which were, I think, first discovered by the OSCE forensic anthropologist if they were injuries afflicted before death to see about the time passed between the injury and the death, moment of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just briefly, we'll go into it detail later, did you find -- did you find signs of injury prior to death?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And on how many -- how many sets of remains did you find that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: I found that on three sets of remains dating, I think, two to three weeks before death, and on two or three others which must have happened many years before death.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And these conclusions are set out in that report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Before we get in detail to the analysis that you undertook and your conclusions, I would just -- I would like to take you briefly through your background and your experience. And with the agreement of Defence counsel, I'll lead you through some of this -- some of this area. I understand that you have a degree known in -- known always the Candidaats that you received in June of 1968. And where was that received?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: That was at the medical faculty of Leiden University. It is the equivalent to B.Sc. of Medics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. And in October of 1970 you received a degree called in Dutch a Doctoraal?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Is equivalent to an M.Sc.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And where did you receive that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: In Leiden as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In January of 1973 you received a degree known in Dutch as "Arts"?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And is there an equivalent of that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: That's MD.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: A medical doctor degree?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Sure, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In June of 1947 you received a Ph.D.?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And the -- your arts degree and the Ph.D., was that also from the Leiden Medical Center?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: All of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. What -- could you just tell us briefly what your -- what the topic of your Ph.D. dissertation was.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: The topic of the Ph.D. thesis was of the embryology of the thyroid gland which is, of course, very different from what we're dealing with today. But a Ph.D. is just to show that you can handle independently and without help a piece of science, and the topic is not -- not the important thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Maat, I'm going to go through briefly your work experience maybe starting from where you are currently. You've told us that you are a professor at the Leiden Medical Center. How long have you been a professor there?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Over two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And prior to that did you have a teaching position there as well?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes. I have been teaching there from 1977 up to 1986 and again from 1993 up until now. By the way, I should also add to that that since several years I spent one day as an expert on the permanent board of the Ministry of Justice at the Netherlands Forensic Institute here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And that's something you continue to do today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In addition to your teaching responsibilities, you -- you're a research scientist as well, I believe. And what areas do you conduct research in?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: The research is on various areas, the main ones being on paleopathology, and the other being on human growth. All of those are related physical anthropology, but I have to add to that that the main direction of research is on the forensic side of that, and especially on the applicability of the methods on these topics for forensic use.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Does your research read to the publication of articles?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: It should and it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. And how many articles have you published?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: I'm sorry to say I wouldn't know. You will have to look in the CV. I suppose that would be at least over a hundred papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, Witness, I'll show you a document marked U0082248 through U008 -- okay. Mr. Younis tells me everyone has that already, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, for the record we're happy to accept that the curriculum vitae of the professor as a true and accurate record of his experience, qualifications and publications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And in addition to those articles, do you speak at conferences?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes, I do, on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And is the detail -- are the details relating to those conferences that you speak at in your CV as well.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: I expect -- sorry, I don't understand. Are the details --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The details relating to the talks or lectures that you give at conferences, can we find that in your CV as well?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: For sure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. When you present these papers and also for the purposes of lectures what languages do you do this?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Usually this is in English. It's only quite -- it's only very seldom that this is in Dutch for the Dutch scientists, but the last years this is actually even in the Netherlands always done in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Maat, you've told us that you're a professor in anatomy and physical anthropology. Could you tell us: What is physical anthropology? I know it may be difficult to summarise simply, but if you could do that, please.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: In the simplest way. It's the study of the development of mankind, and especially for the morphological side of that. That means it conversation topics like human evolution, forensic anthropology, paleopathology, human growth, adaptations of the human body to environmental changes and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And forensic anthropology, that's an area you've done considerable work in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What is forensic anthropology?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Forensic anthropology is mainly concerned about the application of methods developed in the other fields which I have already stated to use them for the benefit of forensic courses. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Dr. Maat. You also mentioned the term paleopathology as one of the other fields you've mentioned. Is that an area you've worked in as well?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes, very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What is that? What is paleopathology?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Actually it is the pathology as it is seen in the human remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Is there any particular area of human remains that is a study of or would it be generally?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: It could be generally. In my case it is mainly on that of dry bone tissue of the skeleton.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, turning to the area of dry bone tissue, what is dry bone tissue?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Dry bone tissue is actually bone where the organic component, that is the proteins, have decomposed and almost only the mineral component of bone is left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And is it correct that the term dry bone tissue differs or can be juxtaposed with the term soft tissue?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes, because the part left out, if speaking about dry bone tissue is the soft tissue, soft remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Is the analysis of dry bone tissue, is that different from the analysis of soft tissue?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes, because the dry bone tissue and also the, let's say the living bone tissue contains a lot of minerals, even to the extent that it is a hard if compared to the other tissues surrounding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Normally who is it or what kind of qualifications would you need to do an analysis of dry bone tissue? What's involved in that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: The person who is studying that is always a physical anthropologist, almost never a pathologist, a pathologist have focused their study very much on soft tissue remains and looking, of course, to the cause of death. And if it comes to the dry bone tissue, then it is the forensic anthropologist who is taking care of that. And in the case of paleopathology, we look at the changes which bone may have from diseases or from injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You explained you did work in dry bone tissue as well. When did you begin doing work on dry bone tissue?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Actually that's in the 1977 so that's quite some time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And who -- are there other people who do dry bone tissue analysis in Holland?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Very, very few. The very few others -- except for somebody who is trained by me at the moment to replace me on the long-term. It is also looked at by archaeologists, but for the analysis of pathologic changes you have to have a medical degree to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So before -- if there is only you and someone you're training doing this kind of work, prior to 1977 when you began who was doing that kind of work in Holland?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Actually, it was not done. The pathologist may have taken a look at that, but as soon as I started to work with that, the pathologists of the Forensic Institute, which was very small by that time, there was only one pathologist, in case he encountered on skeletal material always consulted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In terms of the -- your analyses of dry bone tissue, let's say this year or the previous year, approximately how many cases would -- would you -- would you actually analyse?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Most of the cases come via the Netherlands Forensic Institute in The Hague, and that would be one to two cases every week. And that are the routine cases. Sometimes there are special cases, like for instance what we are dealing with at the moment, and they come with requests from outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And if it's not the -- say most of the cases come via the Netherlands Forensic Institute. If it doesn't come from them where else does it come from?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: In that case it comes from an international organisation like this or it comes straightaway from the police organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That would be the Dutch police?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When you -- and when you talk about cases, what do you mean? Are they actually bone samples or -- or what is it that you actually receive?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: If it is on the regular case it is usually bone samples, but now and then it is a full skeleton if that is found. And otherwise it are pieces of bone samples taken out by the pathologist and his assistance for my assessment and they're brought to the department in Leiden. And sometimes it's about work abroad like, for instance, in Kosovo. But then it is not via the Netherlands Forensic Institute but in that case on the request of the ICTY like in 1999 and 2000 and 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: These -- these bone samples, where are they maintained at the Leiden -- in your -- where you work, are they maintained?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: They are in the department, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And that would be the department of anatomy?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes, that's in the department of anatomy. You have the unit on physical anthropology, which I am dealing with, and that is more or less separate from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Who has access to these bone samples?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Myself and the chief technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Is there any security around your office?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes. The -- there is electronic security on the building overall, and the place where the forensic samples are kept is behind an ordinary locked door within the institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. For these cases, these bone samples provided to you by the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Netherlands Forensic Institute or the Dutch police, is it -- if it's possible, could you tell us what types of analyses you are normally requested to undertake.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: It varies somewhat, but most cases are about the identification of unknown individuals, and for that it is necessary, for instance, to determine the sex of the person, the age of the person, to calculate its stature and see if there are any pathologic changes which may help in identifying the person. In the old days there was done only gross anatomically, so in that case from a person I needed the the skull and the femur and one-half of the pelvis. But these days we have refined the methods to studying the fourth rib for age and doing a microscopic evaluation of the bone remodelling in the femoral shaft for age determination which is more elegant and less destructive for the corpse.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Maat, have you previously testified in Court?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes, many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And in which court or courts?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: In the Dutch courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In addition to testifying, have you otherwise provided the results of your analyses to courts?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes, also for the ICTY on the work on mass burials, in my case in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And will we be able to find some -- some detail regarding these reports for forensics cases in your CV?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes, that must be included in the CV. I think that for sure, yes. It will be under the title of "Miscellaneous," because it's not pure scientific work. So you can't put it under full-length scientific publications or abstracts. It's different. It's a forensic report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Dr. Maat. To the best of your knowledge, has your expertise always been accepted in court?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Up until now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, turning to -- turning to the area, the scientific principles involved for the report that you've done for the Office of the Prosecutor here. My question to you is this: What scientific principles are involved in conducting this analysis that you were requested?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: That concerns three main steps which increase in depth. The first thing is to study the human remains, in this case the skeletal material, by means of gross anatomical analysis. The second step is more in depth, that is an X-ray analysis of the found changes; and finally, it is a microscopic analysis. That is, let's say, as deep as you can go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And when you discuss -- when you talk about these three levels of analyses, what scientific principles are you guiding by in conducting the examination? What are you looking for, in other words?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: In this case I was looking for signs which may show that there is a healing of an antemortem injury showing -- because it's a healing that time has passed between the insult and the moment of death and that are actually growth changes or healing changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, I understand you have some slides that you'll take us through to explain this -- this healing process. But maybe before we turn to the slides if I could just ask you would it be possible for you to describe for the -- for the Court briefly what the main areas of healing processes are, and then we can go through the slides to look at it in more detail.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: In case of fractures, and that is what we are talking about, the first step in the process is that during the infliction of the fracture the fracture gap is filled with blood and edema develops. There will be pain and redness. Shortly after, that is the second step, is debris will have to be removed by the body cells. That is a sort of mopping-up activity to clean up the area to make it possible that healing may start. The third step will be that the broken ends of the bone will be smoothened [sic]. That will help in the removal of small particles which did not come loose as separate debris but were still, let's say, hanging on the fracture surface and will smooth it in such a way that new bone can be formated [sic]. And the fourth step is that in the gap cartilage and bone will be develop. In that phase, that fourth phase, the bone which develops in the cartilage is a sort of meshwork in three dimensional directions. It's rather at random, just to fill in the gap. And the fifth stage will be that the bone which is deposited there would be restructured, remoulded as we call it, in the parallel to the longitudinal axis of the bone to make it more strong. So there will be a change in the direction of the bone fibres and a lot of extra bone will formated like an sort of thick collar around the fracture site to bridge the gap. That is actually the sixth phase, the bridging of the gap. And then finally if it is successful this thick collar will be streamlined so that the bone will retake as far as possible its original form.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. And if we understand your explanation correctly, there is a chronological aspect to this; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes. Self-understandably, for all healing and growth processes time is need.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: It may now be a good time to turn to some of the slides you have and it might -- to streamline things I might direct you to a particular slide. If we can provide an extra -- I have an extra copy of an index of these slides for you. The index for the slides is in tab 2. Perhaps it's not. Perhaps it's here.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And I believe we're going to have these slides on the -- what is this? This is the ELMO. It will be on our monitors anyway. Computer evidence. Thank you. Okay. Dr. Maat, if you could move forward through the slides until slide 12. And we may go back to some of these at a later point. Could you describe now stage by stage the healing process you've outlined for us but paying specific attention to what it is that you are looking for both -- or at all three levels of analyses, first of all, the growth -- I'm sorry, the gross anatomical analysis; secondly the X-ray or radiological analysis; and thirdly the microscopic analysis.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes. As you can see depicted in the first phase we have this hemorrhage in the cleft between the broken ends of the bone. The haematoma there and the swelling and the breakdown of blood as it is mentioned here is something to happen in the first two days after injury. That means since these are all soft tissue components that that phase cannot be made -- can be made visible in a live situation but cannot be made visible with X-ray or with dry bone study because this type of remain decomposes completely after death and will disappear in the grave. In the second phase we have in the following days what we call phagocytosis of cell debris. Phagocytosis is actually a process in which specific cells eat the debris away. That is this mopping up operation I mentioned before. That again is just the removal of soft tissue from the first phase and self-understandably in the grave after decomposition this activity cannot be seen. Then we enter into the third page where cartilage and bone matrix is formated. And that cartilage which is deposited there is of course -- can be seen in the live situation but cartilage will after death completely decompose and because of that the cartilage cannot be found by study of gross anatomy or X-ray once we are dealing with dry bone tissue. Now, the fourth phase in this cartilage bone spicules but dispersed in any direction will be found. That will only develop after a week. And this bone formation which is actually very much an at-random deposition has no -- let's say it is a meshwork but it is not really fixed to the broken ends of the bone and because of that after decomposition you will not find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Maat if I could just interrupt you for a minute on that previous slide. Could you please explain what is a bone spicule?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: A bone spicule is a strand of bone fibres. That means that is mineralised cartilage -- sorry, mineralised protein, collagen and just strands of bone tissue which form a network in any direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And is that visible to the eye, to the unaided eye in a gross anatomical examination?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: That would be during the live situation that would become visible on an X-ray. But in the dry bone tissue case, it is not firmly attached to the broken ends of the bone. It will be washed away with the groundwater. You will not find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Would you find that in a microscopic analysis?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Depends what you mean with a microscopic analysis. If it is a microscopic analysis of the complete body, then you may find that. Or in a living person. And if it is looked for in the situation of dry bone tissue, it will be watched away by the water in the ground. You will not be able to find that unless it is still in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Maat. If you could please continue with I believe stage 5.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes. In stage 5 then these separate spicules during the second and third week, they form that meshwork which I have been talking about. And because of all the cartilage around there will be a sort of flexible union of both bone ends. More interestingly -- and that -- let's say that meshwork of bone fibre strands is called a callus, and that callus is formated not only at the level of the marrow cavity, that is to say inside the bone, but also onto the exterior of the bone, and that is seen as a sort of thick collar of very loose bone tissue. Now, this so-called callus which is there needs to be remodelled, and for the remodelling - which means that the at-random organisation of this bone tissue will become reorganised into a direction longitudinal, that is parallel to the axis of the bone to let both ends meet - that remodelling process is important for phase number 6. But you will need two weeks after the injury to let that happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Maat, I'm sorry if I could just interrupt you again there. What you've spoken about so far in phase 5, what of that, if anything, is visible to the unaided eye in the gross anatomical analysis?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: That will be -- yes, that will be visible in the gross anatomical analysis. It will be visible on the X-ray because these bone strands are mineralised, so they will stop the X-rays and therefore show on the X-ray film. And that can be seen with the naked eye, and it can be seen with the X-ray operators both.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Is that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry for interrupting you there again. If you could please continue where you left off.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Actually, you don't need to feel sorry, because I forgot to tell. In the next phase you get this very typical remodelling process after two weeks in which the at-random organisation of the tissue becomes longitudinal, that is parallel to the bone axis; it becomes better organised, and in that period -- during that period, you will see that both gross anatomically, with the naked eye on dry bone tissue; you will see it with the X-ray as well as a sort of wooly attachment seen onto -- near the end of the bones. That wooly sort of first bone which is formated is called here radiopacity because it sort of gives a whitish effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You mean a whitish effect if you're looking at it through an X-ray; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Through an X-ray, yes. Opaque. It gives an opaque impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us on this phase which I believe is phase number 6, what -- what of these processes what of them are visible to the unaided eye, firstly; secondly what is visible in an X-ray; and lastly, what is visible in a microscopic analysis? What would you be looking for?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Well, with the unaided eye you will look for bone apposition onto the outside near the broken ends of the bone. With X-ray, you will look at the same place, but you will look for this opalesque effect because the X-ray beams are stopped by the minerals in the callus. And in the microscope you will look especially to the direction of the fibres inside that callus meshwork to see if there is already a remodelling activity from an at-random organisation into a directional organisation from one bone into the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just very briefly to remind us, you've given a description of it once before. What is remodelling? What is being remodelled?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Actually, there are two sites in the bone end that are remodelled. Remodelling is let's say a sort of replacement of old bone tissue by new bone tissue in such a way that is part of the healing process. Of course before the bone was broken there was no healing at all. You had a three-dimensional architecture of the bone tissue. And now by the fracture that architecture is interrupted and the body will try to regain that architecture, but it will first do that in a rather chaotic way. As mentioned, that will be done in an at-random way just to get the two ends together with a surplus of bone tissue and later that will be streamlined. Now, that remodelling which is actually the process on a microscopic level means that cell strands which run in any direction will be broken down and built up again but then parallel to the bone axis. And the second thing what will happen, which is mentioned here with the cutting and so-called closing cones, and that is longitudinal inside the bone which stayed intact holes are drilled, so to speak, by cells in the longitudinal direction, that is from the shaft towards the broken end of it. And that -- these channels will be filled in with new bone tissue, that is the so-called closing cone which comes behind the drilling so first there's the drilling and then bone is filling in the gap which has been drilled, and that will happen at both bone ends. So you will get a sort of internal splint because that drilled out part will be filled up with new bone fibres crossing from one bone end to the other bone end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And Dr. Maat you have explained now how these cutting and closing cones bridge the two -- two parts of a broken bone. Are those cones visible to the unaided eye or on an X-ray?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- Analysis?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: These are not visible with the naked eye nor are they visible with the X-ray. You have to do a microscopic analysis. But to do the microscopic analysis you have to make a section, a very thin section through the bone tissue. You will have to make a section so thin that you can look to study -- you can study it with a microscope but so thin that the light will come through it. And then preferably we use not a bright light or ordinary light but we used polarised light. We do that especially to take a look at the direction of the bone fibres because especially this change from multi-directional into uni-directional for the crossing of the bridge is a sign of a further step in the healing process.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Dr. Maat, we'll address again the issue of how you prepare bone samples for examination under the microscope. I had interrupted you when you were describing the phases. I don't recall whether you had finished describing what happens in phase 6 or would you like to go into phase 7.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: I would prefer to go onto phase 7 because the details of phase 6 are more easily understood if you took a look at the real sections, the real microscopic sections.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: In phase 7 that will need at least six weeks after the infliction of the injury. Then this callus formation will see to it that both ends are firmly united. That means that they are only united in a functional way, which means that you could stand on the bone again if you wanted to, but it does not mean that the bone has the original form back. From six weeks on, this so-called streamlining process will happen. And the streamlining process will bring you into phase number 8 if it is successful, because then the surplus of bone, that collar around the fracture site will be removed and the bone will look like as if nothing has ever happened before. That can only be, of course, accomplished if the fracture is held stable so the bone can really become united. If the bone stays unstable and moves all the time then it becomes impossible for the cells to make a rigid, bony bridge between the two ends and a sort of new joint will develop at the site of the gap because there's insufficient rest to make the bridge. And that we call a pseudoarthrosis, a sort of fake joint.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Maat, if I can just ask you going back to stage or phase 7, could you remind us again what the hard callus is firstly, and secondly could you tell us whether that's visible to the unaided eye.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes, that is visible to the unaided eye because it is a firm, strong thick collar around the fracture site. It is certainly visible with the X-ray. And if you would study it with the microscope you would see that this bone collar would only exist of fibres which run from one end, broken end, to the other end parallel to the bone axis. It will not show any longer this at-random dispersed organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Maat, the process of the bone healing which you've just outlined to us in these -- in these eight phases, when were these principles of bone healing, when were they first discovered or established?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Well, if it comes to the gross anatomical changes which you could see with the unaided eye, that was actually a healing process which was already described in the 18th century, so a long time ago. Then in the 19th century, this last half of the 19th century when the microscope was invented. Then the -- let's say the microscopic effect was discovered and described for the first time. And at the beginning of the 20th century when the X-ray machines were inventioned [sic], also of course the X-ray phenomena became visible. But basically, on all these three levels the healing process was already taken into the pathology and anthropology textbooks I think a couple of years before the Second World War and have stayed actually in the textbooks unchanged since then because the healing process has been rigorously studied at earlier times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And more specifically relating to the chronology or the time frame within which these eight phases occur, when was that first established or when was that first discovered? I'm not sure what the right term for that is.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Well, it was first -- the gross anatomical changes were first described already in the 18th century and the microscopic changes were formulated for the first time at the end of the 19th century but more in detail at the beginning of the 20th century and that latter together with the X-ray descriptions since the X-ray machine was there. The X-ray machine was actually of course not developed for -- for the scientific purposes of studying the fracture healing, but were for the clinical people to see how the healing process made progress and if broken ends were really lined up well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: But with regard specifically to the chronology or the time frame after injury within which these phases occur, how long has that been established in the science?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Anyway before Second World War, I mean short after the invention of these apparatuses. It was one of the most extensively studied in those days because it was a very common pathology in life so it needed study to improve the health condition of the people. And so the phases which I have been describing were already described before the Second World War, if that is what you want to know. I'm not completely sure about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: My question was specifically with regards to, for example, the timing. Yes. We have phase 7, after two to three months or after six weeks certain things happen.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: That was settled before Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if we could -- if we could have these slides given an exhibit number we can afterwards clean up the matter of which specific slides are reviewed or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The slides as a group will be received as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's under -- Mr. Younis has just reminded me that's specifically under tab 2 of the binder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit -- the exhibit number for the slides, that will be -- tab 2 would be P198.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And I had neglected also to get a number for Dr. Maat's CV which is under tab 1 of the bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 1 would be Prosecution Exhibit P199.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Maat, with reference to the phases of healing you've just outlined for us and that are set out in your slides here, what is the variation in this process among different persons, if any?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: There is a little variation between individuals, but especially in the steps of the first one and a half month that variation is very little. And that -- one of the reasons is that the -- there are so many steps in -- following short after each other during that phase that you can do the timing in the best way, and this is just actually a full automated healing process by the body which will only, I think, hamper if there's some serious diseases there everything is held up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me if I might. I may have misheard. I believe that Dr. Maat said there is a lot of variation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very little variation in the first one and a half months.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Maybe I misheard. Referring to line 9: "There is a little variation between individuals but specially in the steps the first one and a half months that variation is very little."

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. I believe the witness has clarified that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And if you review the three slides that you have setting out the phases of the healing process, is that variation, that little variation between individuals, is that actually set out in your slides as a range of time for each stage?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: That has already been taken in. The timing is in yellow, as you can see on the schedule, and the timing is always in -- in terms of an interval.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Maat, you had mentioned also that there are some serious diseases where everything can be held up. Could you give us an example?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Well, I think the most striking example is that if people have ask scurvy, that is avitaminosis C, so that they don't have vitamin C in their body, in that case the proteins are not formated and the healing will not happen at all. It won't happen a little bit but it won't happen at all. But for avitaminosis C you have -- you'll need a diet for over half a year without any vitamin C in it, and that is something very hard to accomplish because a lot of food which people take in contain vitamin C.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And is there a common word for that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Scurvy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I what about -- you mentioned before mobility of the bones as something that does appear in your time line in phase 8. Would the mobility of the phones, in other words if they weren't stabilised, would that have an impact on the earlier phases or the time of the earlier phases?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: It will not affect the timing very much actually at all, but it will -- because these processes which happen at each broken end, the end of each broken end will continue only the phase of stabilisation will not be reached in phase number 7. So the callus formation will happen and all microscopic events necessary to do that will happen, only they will be on the long-run unsuccessful because immobility will not give the possibility to give a bridging.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Maat, I'd like to turn now to the actual examination process itself. You've mentioned three levels of analyses, the gross anatomical analysis or examination, the X-ray examination, as well as the microscopic. If you could take each of those in turn and describe what is involved. With the gross anatomical, what is involved in that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Do you mean what is involved morphologically?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Let's begin what you actually do. You've explained what it is you're looking for. How is that examination done? And it could be very simple.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: You just have to look at the bone ends to see if there is extra bone added on to the outside near the broken ends. That is the solid called callus formation. Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's --

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: It's just as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what about the --

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: X-ray?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- X-ray examination?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: In that case you make an X-ray of that end to see if -- of course to see if the callus which is on the outside is visible, but to see if the same is happening on the inside of the bone at the marrow cavity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned that -- a certain challenge in preparing the microscopic analysis. Could you explain to the Judges what that problem is?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: It's no longer a problem, it's a solved thing. But as you will understand, if bone tissue is fresh and you want to study the histology of that bone tissue, you have to make a very thin slice. Now, since bone is mineralised, it's hard to cut with a knife. Actually, it becomes almost impossible to make a nice smooth cut of thin bone tissue for study by the microscope. For that reason the pathologist take the mineral out. They demineralise it in a fluid so that only actually the protein component is left so it is soft. So it can be sliced. In dry bone tissue can not be done because in dry bone tissue you only have the mineral component so if you demineralise dry bone tissue you will only end up with a bottle with -- with fluid, with powder in it. The morphology is gone immediately because there is nothing else than mineral. It dissolved, actually, in toto. What has to be done if you want to study it is to develop a new technique by which you do not mineralise the bone but nevertheless are still able to make a thin section requested for microscopy. This is something we have been working on for some years and solved quite a number of years ago and has been shown also to be quite useful also in this case. To make the microscopic changes in dry bone tissue visible, that is actually making things visible which were already known but which could not be seen in dry bone tissue, only in fresh bone tissue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When you say this technique that you've just described in which you do not demineralise the bone was something that you've been working on for some years, when did you first -- when did you first develop that technique?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: I think I started with that in 1996 or 1997, something like that, and that was actually because I ran into a paper by an American pathologist who wanted to look at fresh bone tissue which samples were taken away during surgery and had to be diagnosed during the surgery. But that was fresh bone tissue and he made a start with this preparation of so-called ground sections, and it seemed to me that that technique was -- could be used for dry bone tissue as well, but a couple of modifications had to be made which we did. And already after short time it became very useful and since then we have been using it already for many, many years. And in my field of science more and more departments are starting to use this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Just a couple of follow-up questions on that. When you say that "we" developed this technique, who do you mean by "we"?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: That's me and my chief technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And when you developed this technique, did you -- did you publish anything about this technique or did you publish it anywhere?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We thought it so of interest to everybody studying dry bone material that the first thing we made was a manual describing very precisely how to do it. And at the same time we have sent it to the International Journal of Osteoarchaeology, and via that journal it was published. And on top of that we have been to various conferences to give workshops to learn the people how to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And perhaps -- we have a couple of minutes before the break and I'll just finish this section with a couple of questions in connection with this technique. The publication of this technique that you mention in the journal International Journal of Osteoarchaeology as well as other publications and lectures you've given, does that constitute peer review?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: But it's not only peer review of the paper. Before that we have given oral presentations on various conferences, and especially during these oral presentations with you are cross-examined by your colleagues if the thing is really valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And have you received criticism about your technique?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Well, actually I've only received enthusiasm about it, not really criticism, because the method was even applicable not only to dry bone remains but also to cremated remains, which is -- which is very, very fragile.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Maat, what -- what does the microscopic analysis, what does that add to the gross anatomical and the X-ray analysis, if anything?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: The main thing is what I mentioned in this phase 6 of the healing recess that you become able to see the so-called cutting and closing cones which cannot be even with the naked eye nor with the X-ray and which is a further step in development; and also that you can see the difference in orientation of bone strands from chaotic into well organised longitudinal, which is again a further step, a further refinement in the timing diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When you say a further refinement in the timing diagnosis, I believe the transcript should read, what do you mean by that, what do you mean by a further refinement?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Well, because in the beginning when the bone fibres are depositioned at random and if they're on a microscopic level in a later phase, are remodelled in a longitudinal direction, that needs more time. And that means that that phase can be refined in its timing. It is a phenomenon which cannot be seen with the naked eye nor with the X-ray apparatus, so it is -- it gives a better timing diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So this is a -- if we understand you correctly this is a refinement in timing that would not have been possible without the microscopic analysis.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes. It would -- it would -- I wouldn't say it wouldn't have been completely -- it would have been possible in fresh bone tissue but it would have been impossible in dry bone tissue like what we are dealing with here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Dr. Maat, one final question before we have our first break. Do you know if there are other people, other scientists who are following your technique of preparation of dry bone tissue for microscopic analysis following -- well, I'll leave it at that. Do you know if there are other people who follow your technique?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes, there are, but not that many. Up until a year ago, I think in Goetingen in Germany this was done -- I think that is -- and north of France at Lille there was done. And actually those were the only three places where that happened. But since that time we have been propagating it at the conferences and into the journals are now coming papers by other scientists who have taken this method into their routine work at the departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that's a convenient time for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doctor, we have to take a break now so the tapes are changed and that takes 20 minutes. So we will resume at five past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Maat, I'd like to turn now to the report that you prepared for the Office of the Prosecutor dated the 13th of August, 2003. Before the break -- well, let me explain this first. I'd like to go through the report looking first at the examinations that you conducted; and secondly, the materials that you had at your disposal for that analysis; and then thirdly, to look at your conclusions. With regards first to the examinations, before the break you had explained to us the three levels, first the gross anatomical examination, secondly the X-ray or radiological examination, and thirdly the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. microscopic examination. Did you apply these three to your analysis for the Office of the Prosecutor for this report?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, moving on to the materials that you were provided. Could you tell us first what was -- could you tell us first or could you describe for us first the bone material that you received in order to conduct your examinations.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: The bone material was stored in Orahovac at the morgue, and every skeleton was packed in a separate carton box.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And Orahovac is in Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, for the purposes of your gross physical examination -- I'm sorry, let me ask you a couple more questions about the bone material. Do you recall how many sets of -- how many separate carton boxes you were provided for your analysis? And if you need to refer to your report, please -- please let me know.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: I thought there were ten boxes. I could check. Ten boxes, yes. That was ten separate individuals and two boxes with so-called surface finds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And where did you conduct your gross physical examination?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: At Orahovac if it comes to the gross anatomical part; in Prizren at the military camp of the German army if it comes to the X-ray examination; and in Leiden here in the Netherlands if it comes to the microscopic observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When you received -- when you went to the Orahovac morgue for the purpose of the gross anatomical examination, did you notice anything unusual about the bones at any point?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Not really unusual. Are you heading at something special?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Were the -- were all the bones properly in their box or did you notice any difficulties with that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes. Basically the bones were properly in their boxes, and I think I have some sort of memory that one or two bones had been misplaced in the boxes, ones that had been filled before my time, which was very apparent because bones that were - how you call this? - were extra, supernumerary bones. I think one or two. And they could easily be put into the right box, these one and two, because they were missing in the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And as far as you can recall, did you have any difficulty at all replacing the bones to their proper boxes?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Were those bones that you recall in the improper boxes, these one or two bones, are these bones that you examined for the purposes of this report?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Not for the purpose of this report. I have let them go through my hands and I have inspected them, but they were not bones with any pathological changes on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just the final question on that: Did the -- did the placement of these one or two bones in the improper box, did that have any impact, as far as you can see, any impact on your analysis?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Who provided you the bones for you to analyse, for the gross anatomical examination in you were in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: One of the technicians of the morgue. I don't recollect his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you had explained to us that the X-ray analysis was done in Prizren; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Who brought the bones over to Prizren for that analysis?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Did I that myself. I packed them, numbered them, and took them with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And if you could please just speak up a little bit, Dr. Maat. You don't have to lean so close to the microphones.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE JOHANNES REINALD MAAT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
